test: Build one row per order job: late-vs-promise flag (first/last shipment after so_line promised_date), late-receipt flag (any receipt on its POs after PO due_on), POs count, op count, est hours, family, customer, year. Compare late-ship rates with vs without late receipt within year x family (and customer), and with controls for #POs/#ops/est hours. Decompose 2016 and 2021 late shipments into late-receipt vs on-time-receipt jobs. Compare yearly/monthly late-receipt share and clocked labour hours (and overtime) with monthly late-ship rate. Check timing: receipt delay vs ship delay.
support: Late-receipt jobs ship late at several times the rate of others within the same year, family and size band; late receipts rise in 2016 and 2021; a large share of late shipments in spike years belong to late-receipt jobs; ship delay tracks receipt delay.
weaken: Late-receipt jobs are a small share of all jobs (e.g. 401 of ~7,950 in 2021), so most late shipments in spike years come from on-time-receipt jobs; on-time-receipt jobs' late rate also spikes (0.18 in 2021) together with clocked load/overtime/hiring; effect shrinks under size controls.
expect: Medium-strong expectation that the per-job late-receipt effect is real and survives controls (rate ratio >3), but that the hypothesis as stated ('mainly') fails: in 2021 most late shipments come from jobs with on-time receipts, and the spike years coincide with high load/overtime more than with late-receipt share. Expect partial support: receipts are a strong per-job driver but not the main driver of the spikes.
